chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from Ibn Muskhan, from Hamzah ibn Humran, from Zurarah, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'Which of the oaths requires expiation?' He said: 'Whatever you swore upon that involves righteousness (al-birr), upon it is the expiation if you do not fulfill it. And whatever you swore upon that involves disobedience (al-ma'siyah), there is no expiation upon you for it if you return from it. And whatever else is neither righteousness nor disobedience, it is of no consequence.'

key_terms.اَلْكَفَّارَةُ: Expiation or atonement for a broken oath
key_terms.اِبْنُ مُسْكَانَ: Ibn Muskhan, a narrator in the chain

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on expiating oaths of righteousness, disobedience, and neutral matters in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: Reported by Zurarah, a prominent companion of Imam al-Sadiq, this hadith clarifies the jurisprudential nuance that breaking an oath to commit a sin requires no expiation, as the primary purpose is to avoid the sin itself. This ruling highlights the Shia emphasis on the practical outcome of the oath rather than the mere utterance, distinguishing it from neutral oaths which carry no penalty. The narration underscores the flexibility in Shia fiqh regarding vows, prioritizing the avoidance of major sins over ritualistic expiation.
